Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion.
Given the undertaking made by the government in the Speech from the Throne to give additional assistance to Canadian athletes, and considering the answer given yesterday by the minister responsible, who apparently considers reasonable to earmark for that purpose a meagre 5 per cent of Loto Canada revenue, considering also the unavoidable responsibility of the government to provide the necessary support for training the athletes who will represent our country at the next Olympic Games in Moscow, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Lavoie):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a rather important matter.
Considering that, according to the Canadian Institute of Agriculture, Canada is on the verge of losing its place among the great food exporting countries of the world; that our country has all essential factors to undertake a serious program of research and development in agriculture; that programs of agricultural research and development are seriously affected by the lack of funds; and that it is a sector as important as energy or transport, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):

subsubtopic: REFERENCE IN CABINET TO USE OF AGENTS-ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It arises out of some confusion in the Public Accounts Committee with regard to information concerning the use of agents, as well as the presentation of documents to that committee. Yesterday, answering a question in committee, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated:
My word to you is that there is no reference in the minutes of that cabinet meeting to any discussion of agents fee in Korea, Argentina or anywhere else.
On December 3, answering a question in the House, the Prime Minister said, presumably referring to the same cabinet meeting:
It happened in a cabinet committee at which I was not present but regarding which I checked the minutes. It was discussed with some of my colleagues and it appeared that Mr. Gray, head of AECL, did mention this $500 million contract, that no authorization was sought.
To maintain the consistency of the record and carry the matter to a conclusion, and since the essence of the matter put to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was how much the cabinet knew about the matter at that time, would the Prime Minister clear up this seeming contradiction?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE IN CABINET TO USE OF AGENTS-ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I have not personally checked the minutes. When I gave that answer a couple of weeks ago I had a talk with some of the ministers involved with that cabinet meeting. Some of

them told me they had no recollection of that particular discussion. One told me he remembered the matter being raised and he thought there had perhaps been some talk of agents-he was not sure, but he thought there was. I am since informed that the minutes do not confirm that there was any talk of agents. I have not personally checked the minutes but I will do so and look at them for myself. Until I do, I will certainly stand by the statement of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
When the House rose on Thursday, December 2,	1976, clause 1 of the bill was under
consideration.
On clause 1-

Mr. Chairman, on the last occasion when we discussed this matter, the hon. member for Winnipeg North had raised a number of questions about the beneficiaries of registered retirement savings plans and registered pension plans, and in particular suggested that deferred income plans of this kind were of particular benefit to those with higher incomes. I have taken advantage of the break in the debate to have some examination made thereof. In particular, I want to bring to the committee and to the hon. member the conclusions from examining the tax records for 1974 which is the last year for which the complete analysis is available. Of course, the 1975 returns which were filed on or before April 30, 1976, have not as yet been fully calculated.
The present $2,500 limit upon contributions to RRSPs, for those who belong to an employee pension plan, is reached at an earned income level of $12,500, which is well below the average family income. The change,of course, was made for the purpose of offsetting the effects of inflation on the limits which had been in effect since 1971. In 1974, the latest year for which the data are available, the average family income was $14,485.
There is a large number of employees whose contractual pension plan contributions, which are expressed as a percentage of employment income, have increased as a result of the growth in nominal incomes and now exceed the limits. Such employees do not get a full deduction for their contributions, while their pension benefits will be fully taxable. The increase in the limits was felt necessary, given the large number of employees who are affected in this manner by the current limits. For the 1974 taxation year, approximately 2.87 million taxpayers claimed a deduction for registered pension plan

contributions totalling $1.3 billion dollars, and 936,000 taxpayers claimed RRSP contributions totalling $1.2 billion.
These figures can be broken down as follows: first, I will deal with registered pension plan contributions. The number of those with an annual income between zero and $10,000 is 1,231,712. For those in the income level between $10,000 and $15,000, the number is 1,020,101. For those between $15,000 and $25,000, the number is 530,845, and for those earning $25,000 and over the number is 94,889. By way of comparison with the registered retirement savings plan, the number of those with an annual income between zero and $10,000 is 229,331. In the $10,000 to $15,000 group, the number is 269,299. In the $15,000 to $25,000 income group, the number of taxpayers is 287,221; and $25,000 and over, 150,535.
It will be clear that a substantial number of taxpayers with modest income have been in the position to take advantage of either the registered pension plan deduction or the registered retirement savings plan deduction. In that sense, it would be a mistake to regard these particular deductions as being of benefit only, or principally, to those in the highest income level.

Mr. Chairman, in respect of the information which the minister has just given to the committee, can he also give the committee the respective benefits which will be derived by each of the income groups to which he has referred?
The relevant benefit in terms of retirement pension secured? What, exactly, does the hon. member mean?
In terms of the income tax savings from the deductibility which they are permitted under these plans.
Mr. Chairman, I cannot give it in individual cases. Naturally, the higher the obligation to pay tax, the larger the dollar amount which will be of assistance to taxpayers.

Does the minister have the average amount, in each of the categories, which will be saved by the respective members of those groups with regard to the amount of tax savings from which they will benefit?
No, Mr. Chairman. We have not done a computer run for the purpose of obtaining that information.

I am very disappointed with the Minister of Finance, who can often be very straightforward. The question asked by my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands is really the relevant question. It is not enough to know the numbers of people who are benefiting. The minister keeps repeating, on these occasions, that he has knocked 1 xh million people or so from the tax rolls. Yes-probably the ones who
December 15, 1976

were paying 75 cents on the dollar in tax. In the last five years or so it would seem so many taxpayers have been taken off the rolls that nobody is left to pay taxes at all. But taxes are still paid. The situation is somewhat like that of a large corporation which announces it has 12,000 shareholders. What we are not told is how many of those shareholders hold 20 per cent, or perhaps 90 per cent of the stock. That is the point we are trying to make-not that some people in the lower or middle income groups derive no benefit from RRSPs, but that a disproportionate benefit goes to those with high incomes.
The present system is becoming increasingly regressive, and there is no greater indication of this than what the minister is doing with regard to RRSPs. He is proposing that in some cases the ceiling be raised from $2,500 to $3,500, and from $4,000 to $5,500. I ask the minister, how many ordinary wage-earners are able to save $3,500 a year? How many ordinary wage earners are able to save $5,500 a year? In this case, the concession applies to both wage earners, where a couple is concerned, so we are talking about a family capable of saving $11,000 a year. This is hardly the small-time proletariat; it is hardly the family of the ordinary man who works in the shop.
The information which the Minister of Finance is putting before the House in attempting to rebut the excellent argument made by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North is really a put-on. I should like to quote from the words used by the National Council of Welfare: "The present system is totally regressive and the minister now proposes to make it more so."
I want to confine my remarks to two main issues: first, the raising of the ceilings and the effect this will have: second, the removal of the 10 per cent surtax. I propose to quote further from an article in which the Welfare Council says: "Canada's hidden welfare system allows the federal government to transfer billions of dollars to wealthy taxpayers through inequitable income tax deductions and exemptions". This is what the article says:
In a report released last night, the Council estimates that 17 "subsidies" such as education deductions and registered home ownership plans cost the government $6.4 billion in lost revenue in 1974 with the bulk going to high-income taxpayers.
A chart based on information from the Department of National Revenue shows the average benefit per taxpayer from the 17 subsidies in 1974 was about $244 for those with incomes less than $5,000.
After all, everybody in society does get some benefit from the working of the tax system in one way or another. What we are contending is that the benefits should be equitable. The article goes on:
But persons earning more than $50,000 realized a tax saving of about $4,000.
That is a terrible state of affairs. It certainly shows that society is not moving in the direction of equality or shared responsibility in terms of bearing the tax load. To continue:
No government would dare propose such a program. Yet the hidden welfare system does just that and there is hardly a protest to be heard.
This is one of the points we are trying to make today. If the government wants to subsidize the rich, if the government wants to encourage savings, let it grant a subsidy and let that subsidy be open, rather than buried in the tax system while the
Income Tax
pretence is maintained that the major welfare benefits go to the poor rather than to the wealthy as is the case with these particular programs. I turn, now, to the issue of the 10 per cent surtax. This afternoon I asked the minister about his intentions. It is becoming common knowledge that the minister has no intention of continuing the 10 per cent surtax beyond this year. This afternoon I asked the minister a question in order to confirm whether that was his position or not. He was evasive; he did not answer my inquiry. When I gave him a further opportunity to clarify the matter and sought an assurance that the stories circulating to the effect that he intends to remove the 5 per cent surtax at the end of the year were wrong, and that he intends to continue the tax for at least the duration of the anti-inflation program, he did not answer that question either and refused to give such an assurance. I should like to quote something the minister had to say on an earlier occasion when he was asked about the surtax placed upon higher incomes as part of the anti-inflation effort. He stated on that occasion:
In terms of fairness and equity, it is, we believe, only fair that those at the upper end of the income scale, who are able to absorb the impact of rising living costs without undue hardship, should be asked to shoulder some share of the burden ... It is fair to ask those who already enjoy ample means to make a proportionately greater sacrifice in the national interest.
Those were the minister's words. The idea behind that statement was to reassure people that while it was easy enough for the government, under the AIB program, to control increases in wages and salaries, it was admittedly far more difficult to control higher incomes and incomes at the professional level. The 5 per cent surtax, meagre as it is, was designed to siphon off part of the extra income as a way of injecting some element of fairness, at least, into this program. The very least the minister can do, in the interest of maintaining some sense of fairness, is to assure the House that the 5 per cent surtax will remain in place, unchanged, or possibly increased, until the conclusion of the AIB program.
What justification is there for the government to continue rolling back wages and salaries when it is not prepared to continue even this small penalty affecting those with higher incomes? Not only that, Mr. Chairman, but by raising the ceilings the minister is proposing to allow these groups to shelter more and more of their income from taxation. Let me quote from the first annual report of the Anti-Inflation Board to indicate that professional income has in fact been rising considerably faster than has wage and salary income:
Preliminary information indicates that on average, the net incomes of professionals rose 13.7 per cent in the first compliance period, from the base period. Table 3.3 provides an initial tabulation of approximately 7,500 reports processed by the end of August. Several problems make it extremely difficult to interpret the data. The measurement of professional "net incomes" does not reflect simply the change in the rate of remuneration professionals receive. The changes in net incomes are also influenced by such factors as changed workload, changes in the type of work performed, and the costs of providing new investment in working capital and overhead. These factors are very difficult, if not impossible-
The word I want to stress there, Mr. Chairman, is "impossible". Everybody knows that if you try to monitor all income, some incomes are more difficult to monitor than others. We

December 15, 1976
Income Tax
recognize that, and this is where the importance of a surtax of some kind comes in. It tries to take into account the fact that some incomes are difficult to monitor and that they will rise. In order to get a program accepted in terms of its fair application, these kinds of incomes have to be treated in a different way from, let us say, wages and salaries, which are very easy to monitor.
Table 3.3 in the same report shows average net incomes of professional practitioners by category. Dentists' incomes show a percentage change of 19.6 per cent. The argument made about professional income is that you cannot say that because it increases it is a reflection of increased fees. It could be that professionals are working longer and harder, though my personal experience of dentists leads me to wonder how many more waiting rooms and chairs they are going to have to shunt people around. I do not know where they get the hours of the day or the extra chairs from to work harder, and this 19.6 per cent has to be a reflection of increased pricing and nothing more. Either that, or dentists have become superhuman overnight.
In the case of engineers, their income percentage change is 20.2 per cent, according to the report. Lawyers are up 14.6 per cent. If the minister wonders why his AIB program has not received the acceptance which he hoped for, here is one clear indication of what every workingman in this country must see as bad faith on the part of the government. The government has sat on wages and salaries. It has controlled wages and salaries. But when it comes to controlling high incomes, not only does it put a very meagre 10 per cent surtax on those incomes but at the earliest opportunity it tucks its tail between its legs and runs from it instead of continuing it for the duration of the program. To ask people to accept that this is a fair approach to this kind of problem is to ask too much.
I want to raise one additional problem with Bill C-22, Mr. Chairman, and it has to do particularly with registered plans and encouragement to save. When one deals with economic matters one can never be certain that one knows exactly what are the consequences of any particular program. But there is a growing body of opinion now-as well, 1 think, as growing evidence-which indicates that this encouragement to save may be saving ourselves right into a depression, that we are saving too much.
Perhaps one of the reasons-and it is only one-that interest rates will continue to be so high in this country and why mortgage rates are so high is these enormously attractive tax benefits the government offers people with savings. All the other forms of investment have to compete with this very attractive form of shelter income. The government has to consider what it is doing in this respect, aside from the equity argument that is made.
I do not buy for a moment the minister's Bell Telephone argument that all of the people buying registered retirement savings plans are widows and orphans, and that all of the poor are benefiting from that kind of program. The very ceilings of the program are an indication that, disproportionately, the rich are getting enormous benefits, or those with substantial sav-

ings are getting the benefit, or those with high tax liability are getting the benefit.
One can argue that even though a program may be inequitable, or that there may be substantial costs which working people have to bear, it is nevertheless a benefit to the nation in some way to have this kind of saving. It seems to me that there is almost a relationship here to the rise in unemployment. Personal savings have been rising very substantially in the five years between 1970 and 1975, the latest period for which I have figures. In 1970 they were 3.3 per cent; in 1971, 4.75 per cent; in 1972, 5.79 per cent; in 1973, 5.62 per cent; in 1974, 5.47 per cent; and in 1975, 6.05 per cent. In fact, there has been this upward movement of personal savings in recent times and, as I said earlier, we may be saving ourselves right into a depression as a result of socking away too much money instead of putting it back into the spending programs necessary to get the economy off the ground. I should like to quote from a news report that appeared in the Toronto Star for December 3, 1975:
A growing number of U.S. economists have begun expressing increased concern that a potentially serious flaw may exist in the west's sought after recovery from its worst recession in 40 years.
The weakness which is disturbing them is savings-far too much savings for far too long, in their opinion.
Those indicating various degrees of worry range from Federal Reserve Board chairman Arthur Burns to academic economists at the renowned Brookings Institute here.
Their anxiety appears to be shared to some extent as well in Europe.
We are living at a time, Mr. Chairman, when standard economics do not seem to be working out; I think most people would agree with that. Everyone is trying to figure out what is happening and why we cannot shake this recession. This is as true in other countries as it is in Canada. It seems that we have to go back to something that Keynes said a long time ago about the encouragement of excessive saving in society-that it is a good way to put yourself into a depression or a recession, particularly when it is done at the expense of the ordinary taxpayer and is given as a gift to the well-off. There can be no justification for these increases in the ceilings on registered retirement plans. Nor can there be any justification, in our view, for withdrawing the 5 per cent surtax at the end of this year.
I noticed, in this morning's Globe and Mail, an article by Hugh Anderson that again raised the question of the need for consumer spending rather than for savings. There was a report of a meeting with economist Jacques Singer, who said that the whole predication of recovery is really one which depends on increasing consumer spending. Saving is always a good thing; like motherhood, it is always difficult to argue against it. I do not want to argue against savings in general; I am simply arguing in respect of excessive savings and the kind of bonuses the government is giving on those savings and the consequence of that kind of high level bribery at the expense of the ordinary taxpayer in Canada.

Having regard to the amount of $3,500 in clause 1, I should like to ask whether consideration has been given, not to changing the dollar limit but to making the percentage limit 25 per cent of earned income rather than 20 per cent, as it now stands, in order that those earning something less than $17,500 a year can take maximum advantage of this provision. Actually, I had an exchange with the hon. member for Edmonton West about this particular question at our last sitting. I suppose there is nothing magic about the 20 per cent or the 25 per cent, but in the outcome we felt that the 25 per cent figure would favour those with investment income. Perhaps the hon. member would like to look back at the earlier answer which appears at page 1626 of Hansard.
Perhaps I could just deal with some of the arguments made by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge. He accused me of being evasive in answering his questions about the surtax. He asked me whether the surtax was confined to 1976 or to subsequent years, and I said to 1976 only. He asked if I could give him the assurance that it would continue, and 1 said I could not give him that assurance. As we explained, this was really a corollary to the fact that as a restraint of government expenditures we were withholding for one year the indexing that would have occurred in family allowance payments. It seemed to us at the time that the family allowance payments favoured, as they do, those primarily at the lower income levels. Therefore, it was those who would have to forgo that income, and it seemed to us it was reasonable that those at the upper end of the income level should also have to forgo something. Income Tax
The hon. member founded an extensive argument on the Anti-Inflation Board report on professional incomes. I would remind him of the answer I gave to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands some weeks ago in the House, that the figures he was referring to were for the first control period-we used the year 1975, 9'/2 months of which were before the control period-and it has not been possible or, indeed, feasible for a number of professionals to break their income down for the last 2Vi months. For that reason, the increase in, for example, dentistry rates in Ontario prior to the anti-inflation program are not good guides as to actual income under the program.
Could I ask the minister a question before he sits down?

Mr. Chairman, I have a comment on this exchange that has been taking place, which I think would be of assistance to the committee. It was my impression that we were on clause 1, dealing with registered retirement savings plans, rather than sundry items throughout the entire bill. Is that correct, or are we getting back into a second reading debate? The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge sort of ranged all over and was citing an article which I thought I had dealt with quite adequately at second reading. In order to develop some coherence, I would hope we could get some indication from the Chair in this regard. Are we going to be dealing with all sorts of things, or are we dealing with registered retirement savings plans?
I would have to concede that I should have withheld my comments on surtax until we reached clause 15 of the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I would suggest to hon. members that they restrict their comments to clause 1 of the bill.

In dealing with the nature of registered retirement savings plans, I think hon. members should take a look at the taxation statistics to which I referred toward the close of the debate the other day, particularly table 15. The minister has been good enough to put partial information on the record with regard to 1974 income. Unfortunately, the 1975 book I have is only for 1973 income.
I suppose all one can say in a general way is that in 1974 there would have been an approximately 10 per cent or 12 per cent increase in average incomes, and a similar increase in income in 1975. As a matter of fact, that is pretty well borne out when we look at the number of taxpayers who contributed to registered pension plans in 1974. The number approaches some three million, and the number of taxpayers from zero taxable income to $100,000 and over was some 936,000. With regard to the suggested argument of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge, I think we can get some perspective by looking at table 15. The hon. member will see that contributions to the Canada Pension Plan are required, and thereby a forced saving on the part of all income earners whether

December 15, 1976
Income Tax
self-employed or salaried: they all make their contributions to the Canada Pension Plan.
In 1973 there were 8.8 million contributors. If one looks at the peak of the chart, he will see it relates to those people with $5,000 to $17,000 taxable income. There is then a dip, followed by a resurgence among those earning over $20,000. If we look at the number of unemployment insurance premiums, again we find this relates to the same group. If we look at the 1974 income statistics and compare them with the 1975 statistics, which are not available, I am sure we would see that the same broad band is involved, showing the increase or hump of the curve at a slightly higher income, perhaps 10 per cent higher because of general inflation.
I do not wish to get back into the argument or debate I was involved in on second reading. I think whoever wrote that article which appeared under the name of the National Council of Welfare misunderstood the nature of tax, misunderstood the nature of earning income and misunderstood the nature of relative deductions. All I can say is that as far as registered retirement savings plans are concerned, I think everyone should be encouraged as much as possible to go beyond the Canada Pension Plan and private savings.
It seems to me that the tax policy in this country should be designed to encourage savings. So far, the philosophy of many people in this country is that if anyone does anything, it is to make sure that the government gets the biggest chunk; that anyone who displays initiative or works hard has to be punished by high taxes. I find that incomprehensible, Mr. Speaker. It is not a question of ability to pay; it is a willingness to work a little harder that results in a higher income. That should be encouraged through savings. One of the reasons we have lost so much Canadian industry and have so few Canadian investors is that people have no money to save. We take it all through taxation at all levels.
In any event, I would hope the government would consider the proposition I made on December 2 with regard to greater flexibility in the formula, and not have just this limitation of 20 per cent but increase the amount to $3,500. I think that is wrong and there should be a much more flexible formula which would allow the benefits of the increases to flow through to all levels of income and thereby increase as much as possible the incentive to save through this kind of plan.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the hon. member for Edmonton West, and it is obvious to me that he completely misunderstands the basis of the argument which members of this party made today and on earlier occasions in respect of clause 1. We are not opposed to people saving money toward the day when they retire; on the contrary, we want all Canadians to save so that when they retire they will have a pension which will permit them to live with some comfort and dignity. What we object to about this particular clause is what we have continuously objected to since the proposal was brought forward.

This kind of provision in the income tax law is an invitation to those who have an income to save. It says to them that if they save the money now, they will not have to pay income tax on the relatively higher income they will have when they retire and will get their pension benefit; their income will be much lower, and not only will they pay less income tax but they will pay at a lower rate. That is a benefit which all the people of this country give to a select group.
I accept the figures the minister gave and those given by the hon. member for Edmonton West. It is not just a few thousand people, but more than half the people in Canada who cannot avail themselves of this kind of provision. More than half the people in Canada will have to depend on three sources of income when they retire: first, on the old age pension, which is indexed, and we have always supported that; second, those who have worked and have contributed to the Canada Pension Plan will receive benefits from that plan; and third, those who work for companies which have private contributory pension plans will receive the benefits under those plans.
There are tens of thousands of Canadians in the latter category, Mr. Chairman. I am not being critical of employers, because I assume they do the best they can, but there is a great deal wrong with those plans. Most of them are not portable, which means if a person works for a company, then is fired or laid off, or decides he wants to work for a different employer, he loses very substantially, if not entirely, the money he put into the private pension plan and which his employer should have matched.
With very few exceptions, these plans are not indexed, which means that when a person retires 5, 10 or 15 years ahead, he will get just the amount for which he contracts in the pension plan. The fact that we may have 5 per cent or 10 per cent inflation each year between now and the time he retires, and that the dollar will probably be worth 20 per cent or 25 per cent less than when he contributed the money, is not taken into account by any of the private pension plans. I am not being critical of them, Mr. Chairman. It is obvious that private pension plans are not big enough to cover that kind of problem.
What we are proposing is an alternative to this kind of provision which we say benefits only those people who can afford to put savings into this special kind of pension plan. We propose that the government should immediately-not ten years from now-look at the kind of pension plan available in some European countries. The other day I mentioned West Germany and Sweden. Both countries have a high standard of living, both countries have fuller employment than we have, and they have pension plans which are run by the state and are compulsory. I am speaking from memory, and if I am not quite correct I am not too far afield. Every person who works pays into the plan. In West Germany, the employer and employee between them pay into a social security fund which covers pensions and certain other provisions-a total of 16 per cent of the employee's wage. The plan is not only run by the state, it is not only universal but completely portable. A worker in West Germany can change jobs many times and his
December 15, 1976

right to an adequate pension is not hurt in any way. That has tremendous advantages in terms of employment policies and in terms of mobility which are things we need in this country.
The plan provides that when a worker retires at age 65 he gets between 60 per cent and 65 per cent of the average of his best five years' earnings. This is far superior to anything we have in Canada. On top of that-and I am sure this will astound the private insurance companies, the actuaries and pension experts in this country who have been attacking the civil service pension plan-in both countries pensions are indexed either to take care of the cost of living or increased by the average increase in the industrial wage for the country.
So when we oppose this, it is not because we are opposed to saving, it is not because we oppose adequate pensions on which people can live in their years of retirement with dignity and comfort, but because we say this is not fair and is not good enough. We want the government to come up with a pension plan which will protect all people who work in this country, so that when they retire they can live with some sense of security, comfort and dignity. We will continue to oppose this kind of tax benefit and what we believe is an unfair bonus to people who are already mainly in the middle and upper income brackets in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few comments. Having been a self-employed person before I became a member, I have come to the conclusion that by and large this is not a good way of saving. I think that perhaps now is the opportunity to ask the minister to answer some of the questions I have for him. I know he will not be able to answer these questions today, but perhaps he could give us some idea of the long-range effect of this type of saving.
First of all, I think we must remember that the government is putting up a substantial amount of money when they allow people to deduct money from their income. I know this will be a major project for the department, but I would like to ask the minister if he could produce some figures for a representative year, such as 1975, if possible, showing what proportion of the money saved and put in a registered retirement plan would be collected by government either federal or provincial. Perhaps the minister could give us an estimate now, a reasonable ball park figure. I think this is important, because if the money is not paid into the treasury by the federal or provincial governments, money which is put into the registered retirement plans but which normally would be charged on income, it means that other forms of taxation would have to be increased to make up for the loss.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North mentioned that people on high incomes would also benefit to some extent, and I think this is true, but it also means that the government would forgo a substantial amount of revenue which normally would be paid in tax. I have my reservations as to this. I believe that registered retirement plans are one of the greatest fuels of inflation because they increase the tax load in other areas. I think the tax system does not really function well if it
Income Tax
does not generate enough tax for the government because of the large amounts of pre-tax savings.
I should like to point out, also, that the government, having given a lot of tax money at one stage of an individual's life, must get it back some time in the future. They will get it back, but inflation will take away the value of a man's savings. Also, in the matter of pay-outs, which tend to be punitive, it can be said that the government will take back a great deal of it in a person's later years. I can remember the time only 30 years ago when a man took out a small life insurance worth $25 a month at the age of 65. That person said that it may not really be a living, but he could live on $25 a month. That is what conditions were like in 1944 or 1945. Obviously, any savings plan based on that is so far from reality now that it is laughable.
The second question I should like to pose to the minister is this: What percentage of the so-called total savings is to be found in the retirement plan? I suppose that would include company retirement plans, and so on. Perhaps the minister could give us the over-all percentage. This would encourage a closer look at this savings feature. Thirdly, I would ask the minister to tell us how many people, or groups of people have this money in their pension plans. I know that people in my profession, medical people, send their savings to the Toronto General Trust where large sums of money are sent from all over the country and put into one pool. Can the minister give us some idea of how large this pool is? This would be useful information.
It is my contention, living as I do in a small town, that practically none of the money in registered retirement plans gets back to the people from which it originated. The reason we have had such urban concentration is that normal savings have been disrupted and that capital is not available in small communities because it is siphoned off into registered retirement plans and taken to the large centres. The same pension plan managers who deal with hundreds of millions of dollars cannot involve themselves in the day to day business of lending money to small entrepreneurs, to small businessmen, farmers and such people. This is very difficult, and I appreciate their problems.
The minister might also indicate what is the limit of lending allowed the managers of these pensions funds. It is my observation that these pensions plans are in the hands of far too few managers in this large country of ours. I would appreciate hearing the minister's answer to some of my questions now or some time in the future.

I would like to take it as notice of a long-range question.
As I said on second reading of the bill and in a previous debate, we are engaged in an internal examination with refer-

How many financial intermediaries are operating the pension? How many trust companies, life insurance companies, and so on? There, again, I suspect that that is not beyond recovery on a factual basis. I can get it. I do not have it today. The hon. member referred very accurately to life insurance companies, trusteed pension plans, whether under union administration under trust company administration, and a whole range of financial intermediaries like this, and on the whole I think the comment the hon. member made with regard to the use these financial intermediaries make of the collected savings-that is to say, to invest partly in government securities but also in the equity and securities of major corporations-is probably correct and that on the whole these financial intermediaries do not primarily make their funds available to the small business sector.
The federal government has moved into this area through the Federal Business Development Bank and through small business loans to try to meet this structural difference in the way funds have been handled. I recognize that it is a matter of legitimate debate as to whether that is being done effectively. That is one of the important questions to which my colleague, the Minister of State (Small Business), will have to address himself, and I am sure we will have occasion to discuss it at some length with regard to the Bank Act.

Mr. Chairman, does the minister, by suggestion or regulation, have any control over the various charges which the various agencies may levy as administrators of the funds established when contributions are made through the RRSP means? Could the minister advise the committee what charges trust companies, banks, insurance companies, et cetera, levy? What is the relative rate of return of each? Is there any comparative information or data collected with regard to where the ordinary citizen, who is not a knowledgeable investor as such, should put his money?

Under the aegis of the Income Tax Act we do not have control over the cost of operation of these various funds, whether they are held by a life insurance company or a trust company. In many cases the rules of operation of the fund are governed by provincial law. All we are really doing is making room in the tax system in which they would operate. I think this is a valid question, and I think we are really not talking about registered pension plans, but registered retirement savings plans where the individual has

some quality of choice. I think it is a valid question as to where a person is best advised to put his money, into a trust company plan, into one which will be invested in relatively short-term notes, or into real estate investments.
That is not just the "$64,000 question," but it is one of infinite amounts as to where the best investment is in this regard. There is a whole range of different institutions, and I think it would be hard to make a comparative examination of the relative front-end or overhead costs of the management of each particular one. I suppose that depends on the skill of the investor in choosing. One presumes that over time, competition will be effective in keeping this down, but I agree that knowledge is very imperfect in this area and that perfect competition is hard to achieve.

Is the minister accumulating any information on that subject, and can he give any advice to the little guy who is not accustomed to investing? I think there are probably many people who can seek advice from people whom they know as to where they should put their money, what they can hope to accumulate, what will be the administrative fee, and what will be the long-term outlook if they put it through a bank, trust company or some other agency; but can the minister accumulate any statistics to help the unsophisticated investor to do the best he can? Has the minister tried to do so, or does he intend to try?

I think the fundamental questions being put are really beyond the scope of any humankind to determine in advance because there are different ways in which people can accrue RRSP benefits. For example, is a whole life policy issued by an insurance company a better, or worse, investment because it has a life insurance element as well as a savings element, than, for example, putting money into some trusteed plan with equity shares in it? I suppose the real question is which return, over any period of time, is going to be bigger in the equity market or the insurance company acting partly in the equity market and partly on its investment in government bonds. I must say that if I knew the clear answer to that question I would be delighted to try to make arrangements in my own case, and I would be delighted to pass it on to the small investor. I think it is almost beyond ability to know. I think I would have to make inquiries on the rather narrow question the hon. member asked as to the relative carrying costs of these.
There were two questions: how much does it cost to operate the plan, and what are the operating costs from year to year? The second question is how well, over a period of time, is my money going to do in relation to investments? I think the second question is almost impossible to answer, although there are many prejudiced opinions around. With regard to the first question, I would have to inquire to see if there has been any private or public analysis on the relative merits of these.

Is there, now, a system whereby an individual who may have life insurance or who may anticipate taking life insurance can consider this as part of an RRSP?

Yes, indeed. With a whole life policy where there is not only a life insurance element but also a savings component, you can, in effect, file in respect to some part of the annual premium paid and be able to take the RRSP benefits in relation to that particular policy. I have just a little advice. When people are doing this, they will, of course, be restricted in their ability to take loans on those policies while they are under the RRSP.
Or that portion.

Well, on the policy, period. If people do decide to borrow, they may find that in the particular year of taking the loan all of it is brought into tax. In connection with life policies , I am not here to tender that kind of advice, but I would inquire very carefully about the kind of benefits which are lost under the life policy if it has to be terminated or drawn on in any way.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister whether, when normally an RRSP would be converted into an annuity, it could be carried in Canada savings bonds and the beneficiary would be able to draw the interest on Canada savings bonds and perhaps encroach on the capital at an agreed upon rate. Obviously, this kind of return is infinitely better than the option which most insurance companies are offering at this time.
Hear, hear!

Yes, Mr. Chairman. The question has been under active consideration, not in the least because of the representations made by the Canadian Association of Consumers. This is one of the questions to which I have asked the retirement income study to give particular attention. I suppose one might put it on a broader basis. If there has been a particular investment carrier, for example a trust company under some kind of trusteed plan, what is the ill in having the arrangement so that that can be continued under that plan but that there would be a pay-out after retirement? It is a question which is being considered by the retirement income study and upon which I hope in due course we can make some suggestions to the House.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to add that there is one difficulty with regard to this particular point, and that is that Canada savings bonds have an accumulated coupon feature. If the interest is taken annually to provide additional living income to the owner, then the bonus after taking the Canada savings bonds up to, shall we say, the market rate is thereby lost. I will agree that there is a considerable advantage, too, in drawing the bond interest at a rate of under $1,000 per year because that exemption would also benefit the holder. There is also the question of losing the bonus for not cashing the coupons.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the minister is capable of finding a method to adapt Canada savings bond issues to meet these circumstances.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad the hon. member for Ottawa West raised that question, since it was among those I intended raising during my intervention in the present debate. I am sure many other hon. members are equally concerned about the question of Canada savings bonds. Certain features about the registered retirement savings plan ought to be reconsidered. With great respect to the Chair, I may find it difficult to confine my remarks to clause 1 since clause 56 on page 62 also deals with the RRSP.
What is the function of the RRSP? The scheme which many Canadians found attractive, they are now beginning to find is loaded. It contains a deceptive feature of which people were not aware when they first decided to invest in such plans. Has anyone made representations to the minister in this respect, and is he prepared to act? Before I continue, may I refer to the question asked by the hon. member for Ottawa West and ask: when will the government be prepared to introduce flexibility with respect to the use of the RRSP? Will this be done in the next budget or will this be done by way of a separate statute?
Registered retirement savings plans have appealed to many who are at the peak of their earning power, as a temporary tax haven. These plans have been looked on by the prudent citizen as a means for building a fund for retirement, when income will be lower and income tax payable lower as well. Unfortunately, the Canadian economy today does not assure even the return of the cash value of investments. We can lay a fair portion of the blame for this on the government. It has failed to provide incentives for industry to grow. Only if industry grows can the value of one's investment grow. Such growth would profit investors. As I said, many income earners at the peak of their earning power decided to invest in RRSPs as a temporary tax haven. They hope to withdraw their invested funds in times when their incomes are not so high and they are in lower tax brackets.
The government has reduced the benefits of this apparent advantage because the plan has been turned into a form of insurance. The government has done this by requiring the conversion at age 71 of the accumulated fund into an annuity based on actuarial criteria. I find this provision iniquitous. Many of my constituents have written to me about it and I am sure the minister and other members have received letters on this subject. My constituents complain about being forced to convert into annuities moneys they have accumulated through savings before the age of 71. The point is, criteria governing such converted funds are different from criteria applying to normal savings.
Why has such provision been included in this extremely complex bill? Why is there not a provision allowing the withdrawal, without penalty, of funds accumulated before age 71, say for investment in some other form of saving? Perhaps the money could be taxable as to dividends but not as to
