capital. I raise this point because the present provision will result in eventual loss to the prudent taxpayer, earner and contributor to this country's economy. At present there is an absolute obligation to convert such savings into an annuity or withdraw the total sum and face the consequences in terms of tax.
I suggest that the current approach to the RRSP is geared more to providing money for mortgages and loans to insurance companies which normally register these plans. As we know, insurance compagnies are always on the look-out for funds an income earner may be prepared to invest. The minister admitted that insurance companies which register such plans unfortunately are not overly ready to make such accumulated funds available to small businessmen. The money is lent to large corporate bodies, perhaps housing corporations or real estate development firms and not to small entrepreneurs who in these tight days find it difficult to obtain funds.
I suggest that the present provisions should be reconsidered. The inflexibilities governing RRSPs should be reviewed. Funds derived from these plans are steadily accumulating in the hands of insurance companies and the money is not readily available to small businessmen and other sectors of the community which need the money. Also, there is a great risk of loss if a person opts for the annuity at age 71, because the annuitant can die the day after he is 71 and so lose his entire savings. Was consideration given to a provision whereby such funds accumulated should go into the estate of the person who had saved, so at least the survivors would have the benefit of the money?
Will the minister reply to the various questions I have raised and say why the 71-year age provision was included in the act, whether there is complete inflexibility with regard to the options open to the saver at age 71, and whether he can opt for the annuity, withdraw his money and pay tax, or opt for the annuity without paying tax; or are there any other alternatives?

Mr. Chairman, may I refer back to the beginning of the RRSP program. As I said in the previous debate, the purpose of the program was to put the self-employed person or persons who did not have the benefit of a company registered pension plan on the same basis as those who had such plan. The hon. member asked, why is the program structured in the present way? It is an attempt to put people in the categories mentioned on the same basis as those who are participants in a company pension plan; hence the annuity element.
The person coming under the company pension plan, normally-I must confess I do not know of any exceptions- would not be entitled to a lump sum payment upon retirement. Under the company pension plan a person would be entitled to a periodic pay-out under the plan during retirement. That is to say, he would be entitled to periodic payments of equal amounts except in such cases as that of Shell Canada where there are periodic payments indexed in relation to the gross national product. In order to put such individual into this situation there had to be some limit at the upper end so that he

would not be given an additional provision which the registered pension plan person does not have, namely, that of being able to choose what kind of assets to put in. That is why in 1957 the annuity requirement was written into the plan. The 70-year provision reflected what was the current age of retirement experience at that time. It has, of course, become much lower since then. At that time the normal age of retirement was 70 years.
As to the options in tax terms, a person has a choice of putting the funds into an annuity on attaining retirement age or having to pay tax, even with the benefit of the averaging provision on the pay-out of the funds. That is his option under the present plan. To a degree, he does have an advantage over somebody in a company pension plan. He can at least take it all out and pay tax on it-but who would want to do that?
In terms of annuities, two things can be said. If someone wants to purchase an annuity of guaranteed term, he avoids the risk that the hon. member mentioned, of buying the annuity plan on Monday and then his estate losing all his capital if he dies on Tuesday. On the other hand, if he does buy a guaranteed term, his capital return on the annuity will be lower than if he is prepared to take his chances. If he does take his chances, in due course he may get a higher pay-out than his capital would have justified. This is one of the things about which none of us can be certain.
It is because of the fact we are looking at a program that was first brought in 20 years ago-the twentieth anniversary will be next March 14-that we are examining this under the retirement study to see to what extent it has departed from established practice and to what extent it would be desirable to give present savings under RRSPs more flexibility than is now in the law.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a brief comment on several things that other speakers have mentioned. The question of the retirement at age 71 to convert into a life insurance contract is one that seems fairly obvious. I am surprised the minister has taken so long with the suggestions made to him by the Canadian Association of Consumers and the National Association of Credit Unions to change that proposal. Conversion to Canada savings bonds, as suggested by the hon. member for Ottawa West, seems an eminently sensible suggestion.
I want to get to a subject that has not been dealt with on the question of RRSPs. I refer to the net loss to the treasury as a result of these kinds of tax shelters and this tax shelter in particular. It has been described by many people as an average man's tax shelter. The fact is that in 1974 it was estimated that the loss to the treasury was $513 million. This was as a result of the difference between the tax paid when it was brought out and the tax saved at the time it was placed into the shelter. This shelter is not enjoyed by the average and poor income earner; it is enjoyed largely by the above-average income earners. I see the minister shaking his head. I would
December 15, 1976

like him to look at the figures that have been developed around this particular subject.
The income group under $5,000 received an average tax saving, as a result of RRSPs, of $1.02. For those earning over $20,000, the average saving was $551.88. The result is that as you examine the income earners and income levels and the effect the RRSP has had, you find that it does encourage savings.
The hon. member for Edmonton West suggested that we need all kinds of legislation which encourages savings. This legislation encourages savings, but only for the above-average and high-income earners. It provides tax credits and tax benefits to above-average and high-income earners. We had better take a look at some legislation which does something for low and average-income earners. Any fair examination of this legislation will show that the real tax benefit and real tax shelter is still among the professional groups.
The net loss to the treasury, as a result of this, is $513 million. If you take that amount, plus the losses through the failure to tax capital gains at its full amount, rather than the reduced amount, and if you take the other loopholes, we are talking about a loss to the treasury of $6.4 billion. That is 20 per cent of this government's budget. The RRSP is just one example of the mess we have got into under the tax system by not having a rational plan or at least a philosophy in terms of a progressive tax system. The RRSP is an anti-progressive feature of the income tax system.
I could go on at some length concerning more figures in terms of income groups and their enjoyment of RRSPs. I know that a broad range of Canadians like the idea of being able to save tax and keep the money for their old age. However, I would ask Canadians to look at the fact that their own tax would be significantly reduced if you unplugged some of these tax shelter loopholes and spread the burden in a progressive way. Many of those in the low income groups would be better off if we unplugged some of the tax shelters such as capital gains where we tax at only 50 per cent of the rate.
I know the hon. member for Ottawa West has read the Carter report on taxation. He may have had some sympathy with it at one time. I may be wrong; it was a long time ago. That is exactly what Carter recommended. If we had looked at the Carter report on taxation we would not have all these problems we now have, with a little shelter here and a big shelter there. When you assess these shelters, you find that it is not the average and low income earners who are taking advantage of them.
Let me go back to the RRSPs we are now debating in the House. Under $5,000, the average tax saved as a result of RRSPs is $1.02. Between $15,000 and $20,000, the average saving is $125.01 right off the top. This is a non-progressive feature in the tax system. I do not have objection to it in terms of the broad range of income tax earners. However, the high and above-average income people have enough tax shelters built into the system: there are all kinds of them. Many of us in the House probably enjoy these tax shelters. However, we have to look at the other end.
Income Tax
One way is to do something unpopular initially. It may be unpopular to cut out all RRSPs. However, I suggest we take a look at cutting out all RRSPs and going to the Carter commission kind of recommendation where a buck is a buck and you tax it as it flows. The result would be a reduction in the amount of tax that the broad range of Canadians would have to pay. Certainly, the average and lower income people would see a reduction in their tax if we taxed dollars as they flowed.
If we take these three items, the RRSP, the amount of tax we would recover if we taxed capital gains as Carter suggested we should, and if we look at the tax shelters built into the registered home ownership program, we would see that the amount of tax revenue now being lost is $6.4 billion a year. That is 20 per cent of the budget.
It seems to me that when we debate shelters of this kind we become involved in detail, as we should, but the principle is wrong. The principle of tax shelters such as these which do not benefit the average and low income earner is one which we should abandon or, at least, if we do not abandon it, we should seek to change the formula under which claims are made. There may be some way of income-testing ability to use these shelters. I do not doubt that those who are able to buy and sell property on a fairly frequent basis are in a position to provide decent retirement incomes for themselves. But others are unable to do so, and in my view we should be making an exemption in favour of those who are financially unable to provide for their retirement years. What the government is doing under the RRSP plan is rewarding those who already have the capacity to look after themselves in retirement.

Perhaps I might reply, Mr. Chairman. First, the hon. member asked why it had taken so long to give the RRSP holder the option of putting his money into Canada savings bonds or something else. Here the question of equity has to be considered. In effect, it would be unfair to the union member to do that. We would be giving to members of this group who, in another argument, the hon. member said probably should not have the right to take the benefit of RRSP, a greater option than the ordinary union member has under a company pension plan.
I believe the hon. member might wish, when he has a chance, to look at Hansard and study the figures I have put on the record. He said the benefits from the registered pension plan have largely flowed to the taxpayer whose income is above average. As I indicated, the average family income in 1974 was $14,485. Of the 2.87 million taxpayers who claimed a reduction in respect of registered pension plan contributions, 2,251,813 had incomes of less than $15,000 a year. So the notion that this plan is loaded at the upper end is not justified.
With respect to self-employed people, I would acknowledge, again, that there is a heavier weight in favour of those with higher incomes, but still the majority of people who are obtaining the benefit of the plan are people with an income of $15,000 and under. The suggestion is that we should cancel the benefit for the self-employed or for people working for a

December 15, 1976
Income Tax
small firm which does not operate a pension plan. At the same time, we should keep the company pension plan for the employees of large firms. It seems to me this would be inequitable, too. There is, obviously, a fundamental difference between the hon. member and myself in the sense that we have provided through old age security measures a basic and, in effect, a non-contributory plan although contributions are made through taxes over a period of years. The Canada Pension Plan enables people to set money aside for themselves out of their earned income sums for their retirement. One could argue about the benefits they should receive, but I must disagree fundamentally with the notion that those who enjoy higher levels of income should not be able to put funds aside. I think it is in the general interest of us all that some of their income should be saved for retirement.

Mr. Chairman, I have followed this exchange with a great deal of interest. The minister has made the point that the retirement savings plan is really an alternative available to those who are not participating in pension plans as members of employee groups. Also, those who are members of pension plans which offer low levels of contribution and inadequate pensions are permitted some supplementation. I wonder whether the minister has given consideration to broadening the agencies which are allowed to administer pension plans. I am thinking, for example, of co-operatives and credit unions with whom the small wage-earner is often accustomed to dealing and to whom he looks as being his financial agent. What is the possibility of permitting institutions of this kind to administer RRSPs as well as the trust companies? It seems to me this would be a much more positive approach than simply denying the benefit of RRSPs, as the hon. member on the other side appeared to suggest, though I should like to think that upon mature reflection he would retract that idea.

In reply to a question put by the hon. member for New Westminster, the minister gave some statistics, possibly from tables prepared by Statistics Canada. Would it be possible to have that particular table appended to today's issue of Hansard?
I have already read the figures into the record.
The whole thing?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to the utilization of the money at the age of 65, I believe there is still some ambiguity as to just how an individual may take advantages of his RRSP benefits. Can the minister give us an explanation of the way in which the plan operates at the moment in this regard? I do not have a speech to make at this point, but I do have one or two questions I wish to ask on this subject.

If the individual has, for example, a life policy which has reached a certain paid-up value, he can, at the age of 65, apply that value for the purpose of purchasing an annuity. Alternatively, he can cash in the

policy, recognizing that he would be subject to payment of income tax. It would all count as income for that year. He would have the benefit of the averaging provisions of the act, but there is no doubt there would be a tax penalty if he withdrew it all in one year.
I had difficulty in following the hon. gentleman. Did he say that the tax would be paid on an averaging basis and, if so, what would be that basis for averaging?
The Income Tax Act does provide for averaging income in relation to tehe experience of previous years. I could give a quick tax opinion to the hon. member, but not while I am on my feet.

I would appreciate it. It seems to me it is rather rough justice to have this whole deal subject to tax as a lump at any particular moment in time. I should like to ask the minister a question or two with respect to a person's obligation to put his RRSP money into an annuity at age 71. What options does a person have? Does he pay income tax on the amount he receives on an annual basis at the age of 71? Can he put this money into an annuity, let us say on a "term certain" basis or some other certain basis so that there would be some accrual to his descendants or estate if he does not take it all at once, or does he have to buy a simple life annuity the benefits of which might be lost upon his demise in a couple of years? Can he, for example, take out a joint annuity covering his wife as well as himself? In short, what limitations are placed on the kind of annuity he can take out? The principle of the annuity is something we understand, but the regulations prescribing it certainly affect its value to the individual or to his estate upon death.

Section 118 of the Income Tax Act provides for income averaging. An individual who chooses to put the money into an annuity will be taxed in the year of receipt on the whole of the annuity payments in that year. However, he can, if he chooses, either buy a guaranteed term annuity or one in which he undertakes the hazards of longevity.

Then he will have the choice of a term certain annuity or a lifetime annuity, whichever he considers best, or both, if they are available to him. In these circumstances, he would not pay income tax by virtue of the transfer of his RRSP assets to an annuity position, except on the annuity payments as received and in the year received; is that correct?
That is correct. There is no tax attributable in the rollover from the RRSPs into the annuity, and the annuity payments in successive years would be taxable in those years.

Let us suppose that at age 65 he finds that he must withdraw some money from his RRSP savings. Is he permitted to make piecemeal withdrawals when he reaches 65 or over and pay tax only on that portion that he withdraws?
December 15, 1976

After all, if the RRSP has a purpose, it is the accumulation of funds which would be spread over his retirement years. If at age 65 he cannot withdraw some portion for that year's use without paying tax on the total in the RRSP, it is really defeating the purpose of the initial savings that he made. It seems to me that he should only pay tax on that portion that he must withdraw in any given year after reaching 65. This would then put it in a position comparable to a pension. As the hon. member for Ottawa said, and also the minister, in many instances these plans are in lieu of a pension. If a man is to be penalized for withdrawing any portion on an annual basis, then it does not conform with the concept of a pension.

In effect, Mr. Chairman, the provisions in the law, as amended by the bill, will not permit a person to make a partial withdrawal. He either has to make a total withdrawal and put it into an annuity plan, or he has to bear the tax cost. There, again, it is a parallel situation with that of the recipient of a registered pension plan who may have the right under the plan, though it is not common, to receive a lump sum payment, which presumably is something less than he would get if you aggregated his pension over a period of years.
If you live long enough.
If you live long enough, that is right. But in both cases it is brought into his income in that year and he will have to bear the tax consequences of that.

Mr. Chairman, I would respectfully suggest to the minister that some scale of regular withdrawals at age 65 should become part of this amendment or of some amendment in the very near future. Maybe you wish to regulate the withdrawal. Maybe you do not want to withdraw it all. But I do not think that a person should be compelled to pay income tax on it all if he finds it necessary to withdraw some, hoping that the balance of it will contribute toward his comfort, say, at the age of 67.

Mr. Chairman, neither these plans nor the registered retirement pension plan has been regarded as a savings plan, like, for example, RHOSPs. It has always been regarded as a provision for retirement with specific benefits taken as retirement income. The hon. member is suggesting what other members have suggested, namely, that it should be changed from being a retirement program to a savings program. That is one of the fundamental questions that we are studying under the retirement pensions study.

Mr. Chairman, may I just clarify a point that the minister and I were discussing which dealt with the progressivity on this particular plan? I think the minister should re-examine the figures which his own department has prepared, because they show that the top 5 per cent of tax filers under this particular plan get 57 per cent of the benefits under RRSPs. The remaining 95 per cent of tax filers get 43 per cent of the benefits.
Income Tax
The minister's point is valid, that in the middle there is a fairly broad range of people receiving benefits. But the point to which I do not think the minister has addressed himself is the non-progressive nature of this particular tax shelter. You find that persons making over $20,000 received, on the average, four times the benefit of a person earning between $15,000 and $20,000. They received 14 times the average benefit of persons making between $10,000 and $15,000. That is taxation in reverse. That is how the poor get poorer and the rich get richer, and it is a point that we think the minister should examine.
The minister has argued in this committee that if you take the average income level there are significant benefits in this regard. The fact is that those in the middle level are still heavily penalized by the amount that goes to the benefit of those earning over $20,000. Let me just repeat the figures. The top 5 per cent of tax filers get 57 per cent of the benefits under an RRSP. That is a figure that the minister should take into consideration in determining whether we should have some examination of income limits, or even abandon the plan.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise a few questions with the minister respecting RRSPs, beginning with subsection 8(1) which is being amended. I refer to the notion of computing a taxpayer's income, and my point is with respect to computing the income of grain producers and their access to the improved provisions under which they can set aside sums for their retirement. A problem arises from an interpretation bulletin published by the Department of National Revenue. The bulletin is described as IT-184 and is dated November 14, 1974. The subject matter of the bulletin is the Income Tax Act and deferred cash purchase tickets issued by the Canadian Wheat Board. These deferred tickets are important to grain producers since they enable them to defer receipt of cash in any given taxation year to the next taxation year, and in that sense level out to some extent their incomes and thus be in a better position to take full advantage of these improved provisions for one's retirement.
The specific problems raised by the bulletin are of two kinds. One is grains which are referred to as grains on which cash receipts may be deferred, and these are the six grains coming under the quota system of the Canadian Wheat Board. That is a restriction that does not help when one is considering retirement savings plans. It may have had some particular purpose when the bulletin was first issued, but the appeal that I am making to the minister is to ask him whether we could alter that interpretation by widening it.
The grains are wheat, oats, barley, rye, flaxseed and rape-seed. The point here is that there are many specialty grains grown and sold for cash, which raises incomes in the year. This may cause fluctuations in farmer income because of the movement of producers in and out of various grains. The appeal I am making to the minister is that the grains defined in that interpretation bulletin include such grains as sunflower seeds, corn, mustard, peas, buckwheat-in fact, all the grains described by the Canada Grains Commission. These have become important cash earners in many parts of Canada. For

Income Tax
example, we need think only of the volumes of corn which are raised. These grains are of particular interest to western producers who are moving into these cash specialty crops in an effort to diversify western agriculture.
The second difficulty with this interpretation bulletin which I think relates to registered retirement savings plans in the sense that income may be deferred and levelled out so that farmers do not have ups and downs in their income and can take advantage of the higher amounts for deduction is that delivery under the present plan has to be made to a primary elevator. Delivery of these kinds of grains that I mentioned is often to processing plants or feed plants or crushing plants. So I think the interpretation requires changing in those two respects. The total range of grains which farmers would have to have classified for the purpose of registered retirement savings is the first change; the second has to do with delivery points.
I hope the minister will take a look at this. If there was sense to the original interpretation, it certainly did not relate to registered retirement savings plans. What I am suggesting is that perhaps we can get a change in interpretation for this purpose.

I would be prepared to undertake that, Mr. Chairman. With regard to the one-year deferral, that was primarily for another purpose, namely, to persuade producers not to hold products off the market purely for taxation reasons. But I am prepared to undertake an examination of the question to see why, if at all, there should be differentiation between the different kinds of grains.

Mr. Chairman, following up some of the questions put to the minister concerning registered retirement savings plans, I notice the minister has likened them to retirement pension plans in which many people are involved. There is quite an essential difference between the two approaches in that a retirement pension plan is, in fact, a general contract in which hundreds, and even thousands of people are automatically caught up, if it is a company plan, whereas a registered retirement savings plan is much more of an individual type contract in which you make a deal with whatever company you wish to place the business.
Would the minister not consider having a little more pliable attitude in order to accommodate the wishes of the people? I certainly disagree with the hon. member for New Westminster who would apparently scrap this program. I think it is very commendable that the government of Canada is encouraging people to provide for their old age opposed to simply being dependent on the state at some later time.
In view of the fact that these are individual contracts, would the minister not agree that greater flexibility could be given? As I understand it, the resentment relates to the fact that this is a shotgun approach in that when an individual reaches the age of 65 or 70 he is required to take the cash out and pay the tax. As the minister has indicated, he would not want to do

that because of the degree of tax, and alternatively the individual should put it into an annuity.
Could there not be an individual plan set up so that a person could shift his cash into a trust to be administered according to whatever he felt would be suitable guidelines for that trust, with the interest and a certain amount of the principal withdrawable over the period of years that the individual lives, with the balance eventually going into the estate of that person who had the registered retirement savings plan? Why cannot that flexibility be given, bearing in mind that these are not general contracts, like many retirement pension plans, but are individual contracts these people have with the company? Why cannot they identify with a trust arrangement during their retirement years?

That is basically the point made by the hon. member for Ottawa West-the notion of putting it into another form of security or annuity. As I indicated in response to him, we would be prepared to consider broadening the kind of security in which this can be held. Indeed, we are going even further than that; we are considering whether what has been heretofore a retirement program should or should not be changed really to a savings program.

Referring to the question of an annuity, I was wondering whether the minister could give the Committee any help as to what, in fact, are the interest restraints the companies set on annuities at the present time? As I understand it, there seems to be considerable resentment. People are well acquainted with the high interest structure we have in this country, that is, 10 per cent, 11 per cent and 12 per cent on mortgages, but when they are applying for an annuity they are quoted very low rates relative to current interest rates. When they complain, it is represented to them generally that these are governmental restraints in order to make the plans actuarially sound. Can the minister indicate what, in fact, those restraints are that apply to those who are in the position of giving such annuities?

They certainly are not under the Income Tax Act. This really relates to the governing jurisdiction in so far as annuity contracts are concerned. The analysis of the Superintendent of Insurance in this respect is that on the whole the rates being offered in the spectrum of different annuities are reasonable.

In view of the relatively high interest structure we have in this country and the high rate of inflation, it may be there is a case for increasing the latitude the companies now have. I noted the minister's reply, but would he at least take that matter into account and give it some consideration? As I understand it, the resentment occurs because of the dramatic difference the people see in comparing the two. A $20,000 registered plan would produce $2,000 a year. People can work that out, and they know they would have the $2,000 plus the principal. However, if they put the money into an annuity I think it can be demonstrated that within 11 years, because of the inflation rate, they will have lost the value of the capital
December 15, 1976

and the entire interest. Compared to that, they would have the $2,000 a year and would still have the principal at the end of 11 years.
In other words, an annuity is structured on such a low interest rate today that there is a tremendous contrast between what you can get if you invest your money in a mortgage or some other interest-bearing security as compared to the relatively low rate required on annuities.

There is really just one comment I can make arising out of the question. The examination by the superintendent did indicate there is quite a difference from company to company in respect of annuities. Therefore, someone in these circumstances would be well advised to shop around in terms of getting the best return. With regard to the reasonableness or otherwise of the return, I think the feeling of the superintendent was that the return was not unreasonable under the circumstances. It really gets back to the question of whether the individual should be entitled to hold his assets in some other way, as trustee assets or otherwise, and receive a periodic payment. That, I say, is a question for consideration.

I have another question which really arises from the point raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West. Is the minister giving any consideration to expanding the number of institutions which can handle registered retirement savings plans? I believe the hon. member referred to co-ops and credit unions. The minister did not say whether the general field might be extended rather than being limited as at the present time.

There is no restriction on co-ops and credit unions except such as may be imposed by provisions under the general law. There is certainly no restriction under the Income Tax Act. Again, as the hon. member knows, these particular institutions are set up under provincial legislation, and without a very full examination of the provincial legislation I would not want to give an opinion as to whether or not they are entitled to write annuity contracts. To give a quick opinion, I would say there is no hesitation to allow co-ops or credit unions to set up registered retirement pension plans and have them registered under the Income Tax Act.

In the minister's capacity as a member of this government, bearing in mind that trust and loan companies' administration comes under his department, is he prepared to recommend that the trust legislation of a federal nature be amended to make it clear that institutions such as co-ops and credit unions would be deemed to have this power to handle registered retirement savings plans?

The federal trust companies' legislation is enabling legislation to provide for the incorporation of trust companies under federal law, having regard to certain powers. The legislation does not in any sense purport to restrain provincial institutions set up under provincial law. In that sense, the enabling legislation of the particular jurisdiction would determine whether a co-op or credit union could
Income Tax
engage in and be a trustee under a registered retirement savings plan and, indeed, could be an annuity carrier.

Earlier the minister said there were few, to use his words, earning $10,000, $12,000 or even $15,000 who could use the full 20 per cent limit. I was wondering whether the minister could indicate why that 20 per cent limit is left in place. I can understand the figures may indicate that there are what he regards as relatively low percentages or there are few earning of the level that reach the 20 per cent limit, to partly answer the point raised by the hon. member for New Westminster who seems to think this was a plan unduly in favour of those on high income levels. But why is more latitude not given to those who earn $10,000 if they are in a position where they can put $5,000 away because of some peculiar circumstance? Why does the minister arbitrarily say that $2,000 is the limit in that case?

It is for the reason I gave at page 1626 of Hansard, Mr. Chairman. It is conceivable, under some circumstances, that investment income would be available for the party to live off, and he could take advantage of an unlimited right available against income for contribution to this kind of plan.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister if he has considered allowing the transfer of RRSPs into spousal plans. Under present legislation it is not possible for a taxpayer to roll funds already accumulated in his own plan into a plan held by his spouse. The advantage of this change to those approaching retirement age, particularly those who have not been able to benefit from the recently introduced spousal provisions, is that they could split their income for tax purposes.

Mr. Chairman, it is possible at the present time, in effect, to collapse one's own plan and have an annuity for a long time, but at the moment there is no provision for the hon. member's suggestion. I am prepared to undertake consideration of it, but I would say that probably, for the reason given in the last few words of the hon. member's question, generally speaking we have sought to avoid incomesplitting between husband and wife. I think the question is whether in those circumstances there might be inequity in relation to other taxpayers.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister and I hope he will consider that recommendation. It would mean both would qualify for the $1,000 exemption beyond age 65 for funds withdrawn for the RRSP. I have another question, Mr. Chairman. On February 28 there will be a scramble to meet the deadline for registering funds and there is a hold-up in filing income tax returns. This would be almost eliminated if the deadline for registering plans could be extended from 60 days from February 28 to, say, 120 days to April 30, after the year ends. Is the minister giving consideration to extending the period?

No, Mr. Chairman. The principal reason is that an administrative problem would be created going right up to the filing date. On the whole, it seems to me the latitude of 60 days is quite reasonable. I am not sure there is any serious inequity involved in not extending it at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, is it possible that we could have a uniform official receipt issued similar to a T-4 slip? This could be issued on the date of investment in an RRSP plan. It would eliminate reliance upon temporary receipts and deposit slips that are of no value because they are unofficial. I have had complaints about the February 28 deadline. This official receipt could also speed filing for people in these circumstances.

Mr. Chairman, this would be an administrative problem for Revenue Canada. I am prepared to take it up, but it seems to me it is almost the obverse of the previous question that the hon. member asked. The delay in getting the receipt is an administrative problem initially.

One final question, Mr. Chairman. The Consumers Association of Canada filed a brief with a number of recommendations. This was countered by the Canada Life Assurance Association. Has the minister studied both documents, and is he planning to implement any of the recommendations contained in the brief of the Consumers Association, or has he given any thought to who is right or wrong in light of the two presentations?
I have examined both, Mr. Chairman, and in this controversy I have referred them to the study on retirement income to which I referred earlier.
Mr. Chairman, at age 65 can a participant in the plan use the income from the accumulated funds of an RRSP? Can he withdraw them and use them for living purposes on an annual basis, without penalty?
No, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, to a very large degree this seems to me to defeat the purpose of the RRSP program. After all, if anyone has accumulated savings in any fashion during his lifetime, he anticipates that those savings, plus the income from them, will contribute to his greater comfort at age 65, or retirement, whenever that may be. The strict regulations which now control the use of these funds at retirement age are a detrimental aspect of the program.
It seems to me it is pretty nearly time we began to get this to the stage where the minister said earlier it was intended to be, namely, a pension opportunity for those who otherwise do not have an opportunity to accrue funds; for instance, a selfemployed, small merchant who might have no pension opportunity other than an insurance program or RRSP. Let us assume he contributes the maximum from a fair wage for 30 or 35 years. It is not inconceivable that he might accumulate $100,000 in savings, plus interest or income of another kind
[Mr. McKenzie.)
which accumulates to this plan. If, at age 65, when he retires he does not even have an opportunity of using the income from this without withdrawing it all, it becomes taxed very heavily. It seems to me that if some flexibility is not introduced at age 65, it is not as useful as it should be. It seems to me the minister has said he has the opportunity at age 65 to put it into an annuity; is that correct?
That is correct.

Mr. Chairman, the next thing is, I think we should have a little bit of flexibility in this annuity. What opportunity is there at the moment for anyone to invest his money in an annuity? Basically, it is the life insurance companies who are experts in this field. For instance, there is no opportunity for anyone to devise his own scheme of annuity.
Let us assume that the Canada savings market would give him a better income from this money than would the annuity market in the life insurance industry. He has no opportunity to get in there. I believe that while we are considering this bill, at least in its application for the next year, it is imperative that an element of flexibility of opportunity at age 65 be introduced. Surely a contributor should be entitled to the income from the money because it will be invested either in a stock fund, a bond fund, a trust fund, or a trust company. Has the minister given any thought to the fact that most trust companies do not have an insured guarantee beyond the level of $40,000 of savings? This dictates that a man with wisdom, in investing money in a trust company, should under no circumstances put more that $40,000 in a single trust company.
Should we not, then, have legislation so that any authorized agent who is to be the receiver of RRSP funds should be insured, as are banks, life insurance companies and others, so that the funds put into RRSP will be protected and will be certain to be there?

That, of course, is a question currently under study by the retirement committee. As to whether we should have deposit insurance up to any amount whatsoever, what we are inclined to do is provide deposit insurance up to a maximum, with general scrutiny by the administration as to the solvency of corporations taking over, to ensure the solvency of assets. Under the circumstances, I am not sure that the additional cost which will be imposed by deposit insurance to an unlimited amount is a real necessity in this program. I can say that in general terms those under federal jurisdiction are well run companies whose solvency is not in question, and in that sense I do not know that deposit insurance should be required up to the last dollar.

I only say that the recommendation has been made, and I think properly made, that a greater number of those dealing in the money markets should be considered as eligible for administrators of RRSP funds. I do not think that if we brought in this new element it would be wise to leave it uninsured, and any area in which these moneys may be placed
December 15, 1976

should be insured. I hope the minister will give consideration to going beyond a certain point and letting people know about it, because if you go beyond a certain point and a trust company is not insured, the money is not guaranteed and I think people should know about it. They should be told to put the money in a second or third fund if they want it used as the minister said it was intended to be used, namely, as a pension opportunity.
It is in this situation that the accumulation of funds would exceed the amount which would be insurable under the existing regulations for trust companies. I wish the minister would give serious thought to it. Let us not leave anybody high and dry when they think they are secure.

Mr. Chairman, much of the well-being of Canadians depends on the amount of savings they can accrue during their lifetime. I do not think that necessarily all the blame rests with this government, but I believe that a series of governments has not given sufficient consideration to encouraging Canadian citizens to try to save. There seems to be a trend in our society at present, which is perhaps due to inflation or other reasons, which encourages people to spend everything they make and never think about a rainy day. I believe governments should encourage Canadian people to save.
One of the areas which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is a roll-over from a company savings plan. I have in mind an individual who wanted to take money out of a government savings plan and put it into an annuity, but the only way in which that could be done was directly from the savings fund into the annuity. In other words, the individual was not permitted to take that money from the fund and put it into the annuity. As a result of this cumbersome and complicated system, the individual lost on the interest on the lifetime annuity because at that point the interest on the annuity was very high. The representative of the insurance company was aware that the interest rate was going to drop, but he could not get his hands on that money; he had to wait until the time when the savings fund was available for transfer. If there were some flexibility so that an individual could put that money into the annuity when the interest rate was high and at a later date take the money out of the fund, so long as it was done within a certain period of time, I do not see why it should cause any problem.
I am wondering what is the minister's approach to these problems. What I am proposing would not be setting a precedent. There have been occasions when once in a lifetime individuals could make a certain kind of bequest or deal of some sort. I should like to hear the minister comment on these roll-overs.

I am not sure I have captured the intent of the question of the hon. gentleman. The maturity date is determined by contract under the registered retirement savings plan. In order to afford tax concessions, he is required to roll it over into an annuity. I do not really understand the problem on which the hon. member is focusing. If it is the
Income Tax
broader consideration as to whether the money should be in an annuity, a trust fund or the Canada savings bonds, that is another question.

This has to do with a savings plan under federal jurisdiction. In the case I mentioned, the money could be rolled over into an annuity, but the problem was that it had to go directly from the plan to the annuity. If the individual had the right to take that money out, he could have taken it out at a later date, because he lost on the interest.

It seems to me that the point is that the individual has to agree in advance on the maturity date, which may or may not fall at a time when the interest rate is high. Here is another situation in which the position of someone with money in a registered pension plan is similar to someone with money in a registered retirement savings plan. It is conceivable that one could give greater benefits to someone who is self-employed than to an employee of a substantial firm. There is a problem of equity involved between the two. I would be prepared to suggest that the retirement income study look at this question, but it seems to me that here, again, when you start talking about more flexibility for holders of registered retirements savings plans you face an equity problem as against the fellow in a company plan who does not have the same field of action.

Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if the minister could give us an indication as to the extent to which trust companies and those administering registered retirement savings plans are controlled with respect to the fees that they charge to the participants of the plan. The minister will recall that not long ago there was considerable concern about the fee structure, many feeling that they were being charged at too high a level.
They are not controlled under the Income Tax Act to the extent to which they are controlled under the general law. I would have to say that under the federal law they are not controlled.

Would the minister indicate if any review has been done by the government as to what, in fact, the fee structure is, whether it has been found that there is quite a range of fees, or whether they are fairly uniform; and does the government know of any instances where it feels that the fee may be excessive?
This is an area where we would be inclined to leave it to the competitive market situation.

Another thing I feel would be helpful to the committee is if the minister could indicate whether the government has made a review as to what in fact-and I am looking only for ratios-the companies have been investing the registered retirement savings funds in. What percentage is going into Canadian equity investments, into mortgages and into bonds? I think it might be a helpful answer because those who

are challenging the program, such as the hon. member for New Westminster, surely are forgetting the fact that a very worth-while investment pool is being created here. I wonder if the minister could give us any indication as to how that pool is actually being invested.

I cannot give any figures this afternoon on the relative distribution of investments. It involves assessing quite a large range of financial institutions, both under and outside the jurisdiction of the government of Canada, as to how they are holding their assets.

As the minister undoubtedly knows, Statistics Canada has relatively up to date figures in this regard, and I hope the minister can inform the committee of some of those figures. As we are on clause 1,1 wonder if I could get a few comments from the minister concerning statements he made at the time of the budget with respect to taking a new look at the whole area of budgetary secrecy and the budgetary process. Specifically at that time he stated that he intended to seek the guidance of his colleague, the House leader, as to the best way in which to achieve a re-examination by members of the procedures we have followed for many years. He was referring to budgetary procedures. Since we are on clause 1, I wonder if the minister could give us a general indication as to what advances he has made with respect to seeking guidance or coming to a conclusion as to some different approach.

There are really two questions here involving the extent to which there can be consultations in advance without breaching the question of budgetary secrecy. I have had discussions, particularly with the executive director of the Canadian Tax Foundation, on this particular question, but because of the pressure of other matters, the anti-inflation program and the fiscal arrangements legislation, we have not been able to bring this to an early conclusion.
I believe the minister referred to the executive director of the Canadian Tax Foundation. Would I be correct in saying that that is Mr. D. J. Sherbaniuk?
That is correct.

In that connection, Mr. Sherbaniuk, in an article entitled "Budget Secrecy" in the Canadian Tax Journal of May-June 1976, sums up the arguments of those favouring an open budget process when he states that-

speechtext: Order, please. I wonder if the hon. member is getting away from the clause when he touches the question of budgetary secrecy.

Mr. Chairman, I realize your point, but on the other hand I am not sure where I can deal with this question in a meaningful way in the committee of the whole. I thought the most appropriate clause would be clause 1 in that the questions which have been raised today indicate that there is concern about the department's approach to the question of taxation, especially with reference to registered retirement savings plans, and the question of secrecy is a much broader question, as the minister has indicated.
Could there be some preliminary review of the proposals which will be coming into a budget in order to hear all views- for example, the views of the Canadian Tax Foundation people and others-with a view to coming to some consensus before the minister actually brings in his budget and budgetary papers? speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member might think he has a good point, but this bill is the result of a budget and perhaps the point would have been better made during the budget debate. We have before us legislation to amend the statute law relating to income tax, specifically clause 1. I understand the concern of the hon. member, and this is why I allowed him to touch on the subject matter, but to go deeper and start an exchange of opinion with the minister as to budgetary secrecy or as to the presentation of budgets I think is going too far from the clause before us. However, in the meantime I must ask him to come as quickly as possible to the subject matter of clause 1.

Dealing, then, with clause 1, perhaps I could put a question to the minister. Would he have felt it helpful in drafting the proposals which are now before us and as embodied in clause 1 if there had been an independent tax board which, like the Auditor General's office or the public accounts committee, would lie within the parliamentary system, but this independent tax board would be something along the lines of the suggestion of Mr. Sherbaniuk, in order to give some type of preview of what the relative options are, in the case of clause 1, dealing with registered retirement savings plan aspects of the income tax legislation?

It is very hard to say whether that would have been helpful in this case.

Mr. Chairman, I should say to the hon. member for York-Simcoe that that is what this debate is all about. There is no such thing as an independent tax board. Every tax which is levied affects somebody in a different way, and I cannot think of any board which could be put together, which would reach a consensus outside parliament on who gets benefits and who is deprived of them.
This is before the fact.

I wonder who the hon. member for York-Simcoe would put on the board. Would he appoint just bankers and investment dealers in Canada? If we appoint members from the Canadian Labour Congress to that board, there would be no more agreement on the board than we get here, because they are obviously not going to see things the same way. I am sure the investment dealers might find some community of interest in suggesting some changes to the minister. However, that is an aside and I suppose I really should direct my question to the minister. I would like to follow up on some of the questions which have been asked of the Minister of Finance regarding the briefs of the Consumers' Association and, more particularly, the brief from the credit unions. The minister has indicated he has read the brief of the Consumers' Association and also the rebuttal from the Life Insurance Association, and I wonder whether he has seen the significant difference in the brief of the Consumers' Association regarding the disposition of the plans at age 71 in this way.
Credit unions suggest that since the holders of plans may die before they cash in their plans, and since there is no federal estate tax which is commensurate with the income tax schedule, present provisions would confer a benefit on those who receive moneys from the estate. They therefore suggest, in contrast to what was suggested by the Consumers' Association, that if the minister decides to change the options available at age 71, he should make sure that such moneys are taxed at the marginal rate of the person who owns the plan as if he were subject to tax prior to death, in order to avoid any loss to the federal treasury. Has the minister examined the proposals, and is he prepared to consider, in his review, the two proposals before him?
Mr. Chairman, I would be prepared to have them considered in that context.

Mr. Chairman, a multitude of questions has been asked and the minister has been most co-operative with his answers. Although we are in the early stages of a plan which is to last many years, we have reached the point at which we must provide individual savers under this plan with some flexibility of choice and freedom to plan. Certain people will save money for up to 25 years, say, and invest it. By the time they reach age 65 they may have accumulated, by way of capital gains, dividends or other methods, a fair bit of money for retirement.
Income Tax
It is regrettable that the government should say to such people who reach age 65, "If you remove this money from the plan, you will have to average your income tax. We will not allow you to average forward." I understand one may average back four years, and forward one year. If the saver worked all his life, his income was probably greatest just before age 65; probably that is when he paid most income tax. Therefore, requiring him to average back four years, when he paid most income tax, would discourage his participation in the plan.
If the plan is reviewed, we must introduce new concepts to make it work. We should not apply the concept of income tax to pension plan money. Rather, we should be governed by the concept of the maximum good for all, a concept which should apply both to the individual who has saved money, and to the state. If a man chooses not to buy an annuity at age 65, the state should not come to him with its hand out, ready to grab the maximum from him. We should allow the investor to place his RRSP funds with a trust company, for example, which could use the money to secure a mortgage. Over 25 years, such mortgage might provide a secure, reasonable return. Perhaps the saver could do this through a lawyer or other agent who could invest money in absolutely secure property. On reflection, perhaps a trust company is a better agent because of its insured position. At present, existing government income tax laws and regulations discourage individuals from putting all their eggs in one basket.
I should like one question to be clarified. Let us assume a person at age 65 places money in an annuity. What proportion of the money is taxed? Is the entire amount received taxable? Is every payment taxable? Is any part of the money considered as capital, or is it all considered as income in the year in which annuity payments are made? I hope the minister will not in future follow the narrow path with respect to the RRSP program presently being followed. Alternative methods of investing should be considered, methods other than the simple annuity.
I am not aware of companies other than insurance companies from which one can buy an annuity. Thus, a group of companies has a corner on business which should be shared with other companies. Such a corner removes what the minister calls the competitive aspect. He has suggested that charges for administered RRSP programs will be established by competition in the marketplace.
Unfortunately, there is little competition in the annuities market. Therefore, we should give investors several alternative opportunities for so investing their money. For example, the government sells bonds, some of which mature, say, in 1979. The government must pay interest on the money it borrows. Could not such an investment on the part of an individual be considered as an annuity? Not long ago the government adjusted upward the low rate of interest it paid on old, outstanding annuities. Since the government pays 2 per cent or 3 per cent more on Canada savings bonds than insurance companies pay on annuities, why could the government not accept money from the RRSP investor and consider such money as an investment in a government annuity? After all,

the interest it must pay is comparable to what it must pay for other funds it needs to finance its operations.
The government raises money through bonds, and sometimes it must refund money. I submit that the government could be just as flexible with regard to an annuity structure as it is with regard to Canada savings bonds. There is no assurance, when the government floats $1 billion worth of Canada savings bonds, that the bonds will stay in the hands of the original individual investors. To discourage the cashing in of such bonds, the government offers a relatively high rate of interest and guarantees immediate liquidity. I therefore suggest that such bonds could provide an alternative investment for the RRSP investor. The government could easily change the rules and regulations governing the situation. Am I interfering with the next ceremony, Mr. Chairman? Is Black Rod at the door?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member may carry on.

More than ever, the government is encouraging people to manage their money. If we are attempting to help people manage their money, we must do so. At the same time, we must assure the RRSP investor who is looking forward to an assured income in later years of flexibility in the management of his money. I hope the minister will consider introducing legislation in the near future for encouraging ever more people to participate in the RRSP program. It is an advantage; it does accumulate funds. Some of these funds go into the speculative market; they go into the bond market; they are satisfying a real need in Canadian money circles. Having satisfied this need, and having served the country while at the same time serving themselves, the government should introduce flexibility so that the individual can have an opportunity to serve himself to the best possible advantage when the maturity time comes for these moneys.
The annuity and the compulsory movement in an annuity is not good. I would again ask the minister to be more flexible. Let us get out of the compulsive aspect of what can be done with this money, and get into a flexible position. Accordingly, it must be regulated by government and regulated in a fashion ensuring income to keep the man as comfortable as he hoped he might have been. There should not be a single road down which this money has to flow by regulation of government, when there are so many alternatives that offer reasonable security for any man with money at any moment in time.
If this program were 25 years old today, instead of five or six, we would get a great deal more support for the demand on the minister to give these considerations, because at that moment in time, at 25 years old, the amount of money put into RRSPs will be very substantial. The amount of penalty that can be imposed under these regulations for the emergent need of money can be excessive. The regulation which says it must all come out at any moment in time, regardless of the emergency in which the individual finds himself, is not good: it is

too rigid, too strict. I do not think the ordinary individual who is putting money into this program realizes the strictures which this puts on the structure.
As this act is considered, and as future amendments and requirements are considered for this purpose, let us give some thought to the idea that most people putting money into this expect that it will be available for emergencies. Let us give an emergent opportunity for people to use it. Let us give people, within proper regulations and elements of safety, an alternate way of investing in what they may consider to be their best interests and keep tabs on the fact that this money is used in the best possible way.
It is imperative that we get away from the narrow confines of regulations and legislation which keep us going down such a straight line at the minister's demand or at the demand of regulation which may be made in connection with the tax structure.

Mr. Chairman, I have one short question which has to do with double-taxation. I realize the minister has made arrangements with other countries in order that there will be no double-taxation. However, there seems to be within the RRSP a way that on occasion principals are caught with double-taxation. It has to do with the amount paid in. Income tax is not paid until the end of April. However, the funds have to go into the plan prior to the end of February. The money that goes into the plan may be greater than what is allowed by the Income Tax Act. That money is left in there. I realize it can be used in the next year if the participant recognizes this. However, when they make out their income tax form at the end of April, they have to pay income tax on that portion over and above what the RRSP allows, to the amount that they put in.
If that money is taken out of the plan after April 30, they are again taxed on it. Therefore, that portion of the money is taxed twice. Could the department not bring in a plan to negate this? It seems to be unfair. The situation has developed as a result of misunderstanding. Possibly the allowable amount could be increased rather than held at 20 per cent. Will the minister give consideration to this question so that those who are caught in this situation do not pay double taxation on that portion of the money taken out?
Mr. Speaker, there are, indeed, provisions in this bill dealing with the situation of overpayment. I will be glad to deal with this matter when we get to that point.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether Black Rod will stay away long enough to let me say what I want to say. At least I can start. A good many times in this discussion on clause 1 the Minister of Finance has referred to what I believe he calls the retirement committee. I believe that is a committee of persons from the Department of Finance, the Department of National Health and Welfare and Treasury Board which is engaged in an overall discussion on pensions, presumably from all aspects.
December 15, 1976

In my view, this whole discussion on registered retirement savings plans raises a question which I would like to put to the minister. Fundamentally, I suppose I am asking him whether the committee to which he has referred is discussing this aspect of it. However, let me take a moment to outline what I have in mind. I may say I am glad to see the hon. member for Eglinton in his place. If my memory serves me correctly, I can call him as a witness for a proposition I should like to present.
There is a school of thought with respect to pensions which contends that in actual fact pensions are not paid out of savings from the past but are paid out of current production. After all those who live on pensions purchase food, clothing and various services. These are not things that have been saved. These things are being purchased at the present time. In other words, if a person had a pension of $1 million a year and the current society were not producing food, clothing and services, his pension would not be worth anything to him. That raises the whole question as to whether pensions based on accumulated funds are the best way to provide for retirement or whether we should be realistic, realize that pensions are paid out of current production and develop our pension plans accordingly.
This school of thought-and I happen to concur with it- takes the view that these many funds we have, whether the public service superannuation fund or the various other funds the government operates, or funds put away by private employers, or funds which are saved through RRSPs, are really just a way of deciding how much of current production a retired person is to receive. Therefore, those who think in these terms ask, should we not come directly to grips with this issue and decide as a society how much our people are to get by way of pensions. I guess I shall have to deal with this tomorrow.
Progress reported.
